# The Architecture 2.0 Reviewer's Checklist {#sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist}

Evaluating AI-assisted architecture research requires a rigorous rubric to assess methodology, reproducibility, and physical validity. This checklist gives program committee members, peer reviewers, and authors auditing their own work a set of pass/fail questions, ordered by the evidence flow of a bounded study: what was claimed, what ran, what measured it, what could reject it, and who answers for it. A submission can fail an item and still merit publication, but the reviewer should know it failed and the paper should say so.

This checklist is not a second schema. It is the design-loop card of
@sec-architecture-20-ontology read from the outside. The card is what an author
fills in while running a study; the checklist is what a reviewer asks of it
afterward, and the sections below work through the same material in the order a
reviewer meets it. Scope the Claim interrogates intent, task, and design space;
Verify the Environment covers the environment; Check State covers representation;
Identify the Method Roles covers method role; the proxy, baseline, and statistics
sections all interrogate evidence; Trace Rejection Authority covers the rejection
checks and the retained failed runs; Fix the Commitment Boundary covers what the
evidence supports; and Test Ownership covers the accountable decision. The
correspondence is not one to one. A reviewer meets the environment before the
representation, some sections here have no single field behind them, and the
card's feedback budget survives only as a cost reported afterward in Report the
True Cost of Search, never as the allowance a study was supposed to declare
before it spent anything. A study whose card is honestly filled should survive
this list; one that cannot answer an item here usually has an empty field there.

## Scope the Claim

A claim that names no boundaries cannot be reviewed against them (@sec-architecture-20-ontology).

*   **[ ] The bounded task:** Is the design task stated with its workload, design space, objectives, and constraints, so a reader can tell which results the claim covers and which it does not?
*   **[ ] The validity region:** Does the paper state where the claim stops, including the workloads, process assumptions, and operating conditions under which the result was never tested?

## Verify the Environment and Reproducibility

An AI model evaluated without its execution environment cannot be reviewed or reproduced, and publishing model weights without the constraints that bounded them leaves later researchers no faithful way to rerun the study as evaluated.

*   **[ ] The artifact:** Is the full evaluation environment (wrapper, state representations, reward functions, exact simulator versions) released, rather than just the model weights?
*   **[ ] The constraints:** Are the baseline heuristics, design limits, and constraints codified in the released environment rather than hidden as tacit knowledge in private scripts?

## Check State and Data Provenance

What a model learned from decides what its evaluation can establish (@sec-data-representations-world-models).

*   **[ ] The representation:** Is the design-state representation, feature set, or trace corpus sourced, versioned, and scoped, and does its coverage match the design space the claim ranges over?
*   **[ ] The contamination check:** Was the evaluation screened for training-data contamination? Workloads heavily represented in public corpora (matrix multiplication, AES, standard RISC-V cores) test memorization rather than zero-shot architectural exploration [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated].
*   **[ ] The transfer claim:** If the method is learned rather than searched per instance, are the evaluation designs disjoint from everything the model was pretrained or fine-tuned on, and did every arm enter the comparison under the same pretraining condition? A pretrained method beating from-scratch baselines on designs adjacent to its training corpus demonstrates transfer of the corpus, not superiority of the method.

## Identify the Method Roles

A reviewer cannot judge feedback validity without knowing which component produced it (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

*   **[ ] The roles:** Does the paper name the functional role of each AI component, generator, surrogate, optimizer, critic, or verifier, rather than describing a monolithic "AI" or "agent"?
*   **[ ] The decomposition:** If the system composes several roles, is each role's input, output, and authority stated, so a reviewer can see which component's error would corrupt which result?

## Separate Proxy Metrics from Physical Oracles

Reviewers cannot prevent reward hacking, but they can check whether reported optimizations respect physical reality rather than exploiting simulator inaccuracies [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete].

*   **[ ] The proxy boundary:** Does the paper distinguish the fast surrogate metric used for search from the ground-truth oracle used for validation?
*   **[ ] The independence check:** For large claimed gains, did a higher-fidelity stage of the flow, such as RTL synthesis or timing closure, confirm the result did not exploit a simulator loophole? A downstream stage of the same flow shares systematic error with an earlier-stage proxy, so a check drawn from an instrument independent of that flow is stronger still.
*   **[ ] The proxy calibration:** Is the proxy's rank fidelity against ground truth reported in the region where the search actually concentrated, not averaged over the whole space (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect)?
*   **[ ] The correctness check:** Was functional correctness established, by equivalence checking against a golden reference or verification at stated coverage, before any quality-of-results number was claimed for the artifact? A netlist that fails equivalence has no meaningful area, power, or frequency; a pass@k score on lint-clean but unverified RTL measures fluency, not design.

## Match the Baselines and the Budget

Reported gains must come from the method, not from an uneven comparison.

*   **[ ] The baseline control:** Is the method compared against random search, Bayesian optimization, or industry heuristics operating in the same constrained environment?
*   **[ ] The other axes:** Are all objective axes, performance, power, and area at minimum, reported at the same operating point and under the same constraint files, tool versions, and corners for every arm? A frequency gain with unreported area, or arms synthesized under different constraints, is a trade presented as a win. If the claim is single-axis, the comparison must hold everything else equal.
*   **[ ] The budget parity:** Did every arm receive the same evaluation budget, and comparable tuning effort? A tuned method against default-configuration baselines is not a comparison.
*   **[ ] The exploratory split:** Are exploratory runs, where parameters were tuned, separated from confirmatory runs, where the locked design met unseen workloads (@sec-running-the-loop)?

## Demand Statistical Rigor

Learning-based results, deep reinforcement learning especially, are notoriously sensitive to seeds, hyperparameters, and implementation details [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL].

*   **[ ] The sample size:** Are the number of runs, seeds, and model invocations stated, with confidence intervals on headline numbers rather than single best runs?
*   **[ ] The distribution:** For heavy-tailed or bimodal outcomes, are medians and interquartile ranges reported alongside or instead of means?
*   **[ ] The noise floor:** Was the evaluation flow's own replication variance measured, by rerunning the unmodified baseline through the same tools with different seeds, and does the claimed gain exceed it? Commercial synthesis and place-and-route shift timing and power by a few percent on seed changes alone. A gain inside that band is a measurement of the instrument, not of the method.
*   **[ ] The aggregation:** Are normalized results such as speedups and ratios summarized with the geometric mean rather than the arithmetic mean, whose value depends on the choice of reference [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie] (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect)?

## Trace Rejection Authority

The book's central review question applies verbatim to any submission (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

*   **[ ] The rejecting instrument:** Did an independent mechanism have authority to reject the method's output, and is each check declared advisory or blocking? Consensus among correlated models is not independence.
*   **[ ] The negative record:** Are rejected candidates, failed runs, and out-of-distribution failures reported, so the search's true difficulty is visible?

## Fix the Commitment Boundary

Every claim commits at some fidelity, and the paper must not spend above it.

*   **[ ] The evidence level:** Is the fidelity at which the claim commits declared on the fidelity pyramid @sec-data-representations-world-models sets out, running from analytical models through trace-driven and cycle-level simulation to RTL, emulation, and silicon? Physical signoff is a separate axis rather than a tier on that pyramid (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces), so a claim that depends on it should name it too. Does any sentence in the paper claim more than the declared level supports?
*   **[ ] The reopening conditions:** Does the paper state what future observation (workload shift, tool version, silicon measurement) would invalidate the recommendation?

## Require Provenance and Replay

A result that cannot be re-run cannot be reviewed, only believed.

*   **[ ] The replay path:** Can a reader identify the exact executed candidate and tool path, and rerun the recorded computation (@sec-running-the-loop)? Replay is not independent validation, but without it nothing else can be checked.
*   **[ ] The model identity:** Is the model pinned by version and date rather than a floating alias?

## Test Ownership

Accountability questions from @sec-what-architect-owns that a reviewer can ask of any claimed autonomous result:

*   **[ ] The assignment:** Can the paper's authors say who set the scope, authorized the automated actions, judged evidence sufficiency, and made the final call?
*   **[ ] The capacity:** Could that named owner realistically have caught a failure, given the volume of automated decisions they nominally supervised?

## Report the True Cost of Search

A result is only as impressive as the budget that found it.

*   **[ ] The search bill:** Does the paper account for the simulator hours, API calls, licenses, and compute consumed to find the result, compared against what a human baseline would have spent?
*   **[ ] The amortized bill:** For learned methods, is the pretraining or fine-tuning cost amortized into the comparison rather than treated as free?
*   **[ ] The human bill:** Is the human cost of steering the search, including discarded prompts and iterations, accounted for rather than hidden?

## The Limits of the Checklist

Ultimately, this checklist demands transparency in evaluation, but it does not replace engineering judgment. Whatever role the AI plays, generator, surrogate, optimizer, critic, or verifier, no checklist item can substitute for final physical signoff. A candidate geometry, RTL block, or memory schedule that clears every box above still owes its validation to the human architect who must guide it through the actual hardware design flow.
